pharm: A long-chain (C16) fatty alcohol used as an emollient, emulsion stabilizer, and stiffening agent in topical and some oral formulations; pharmacologically inert and not systemically active.

summary: Cetyl alcohol is a waxy, white fatty alcohol (cetanol, C16) used widely as a pharmaceutical and cosmetic excipient - as an emollient, emulsifier, emulsion stabilizer, and stiffening (hardening) agent in creams, lotions, ointments, and some tablets/suppositories. It is not a therapeutic drug and has no intrinsic pharmacological activity. It is generally well tolerated; the main concern is occasional contact allergy or skin irritation, particularly in patients sensitized to fatty alcohols or in stasis dermatitis/leg ulcers.
indications: Pharmaceutical excipient: emulsifying agent, emulsion stabilizer, and stiffening agent in topical and oral dosage forms
Emollient component of skin creams, lotions, and ointments to soften and smooth skin

dosage.d: Present as a formulation excipient at concentrations typically 2-10% (emulsifying/stiffening); apply finished product as directed
Apply the finished emollient product to affected skin as needed
Used as an excipient (stiffening agent); no therapeutic dose

admin: Use the finished pharmaceutical or cosmetic product as labeled
For emollient use, apply a thin layer to clean skin
Avoid applying products to broken or infected skin unless directed
Discontinue if local irritation or rash develops
As an excipient it is incorporated by the manufacturer; no preparation by the user is needed
moa: Cetyl alcohol has no pharmacodynamic (drug) mechanism of action. As an excipient, its amphiphilic structure (a long lipophilic carbon chain with a polar hydroxyl group) lets it function at oil-water interfaces: it acts as a co-emulsifier and emulsion stabilizer, increases the viscosity and consistency of creams and ointments (stiffening agent), and provides emollient/occlusive properties that soften skin and reduce transepidermal water loss.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity/contact allergy to cetyl alcohol or other fatty alcohols
relative: History of contact dermatitis to emulsifying agents
Application to weeping or eczematous skin in sensitized individuals
monitor: Local skin reactions (irritation, rash, contact dermatitis)

preg: Cetyl alcohol used as a topical excipient is considered safe in pregnancy; it is not systemically absorbed in clinically meaningful amounts.
lact: Considered safe during breastfeeding as a topical excipient. If applied near the breast, clean the area before nursing to avoid the infant ingesting the product.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed; cetyl alcohol is essentially not systemically absorbed when used topically.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is needed; cetyl alcohol is essentially not systemically absorbed when used topically.

minor: As an excipient, it has no clinically significant drug interactions
interactions.food: Not relevant for an excipient/topical agent.
interactions.alcohol: Not relevant; cetyl alcohol is a fatty (cetyl) alcohol, not ingestible ethanol, and does not interact with alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: Does not interfere with laboratory tests.

rare: Skin irritation, erythema, or itching at the application site
Worsening of stasis dermatitis/leg ulcers in fatty-alcohol-sensitive patients

monitoring: Observe for local skin irritation or allergic contact dermatitis with repeated use

Tell your pharmacist if you have a known allergy to fatty alcohols or emulsifying ointments
Store the finished product as directed on its label

Not applicable as a therapeutic agent

pearls: Cetyl alcohol is an excipient (cetanol), not a therapeutic drug - it has no dosing or pharmacological activity
Despite 'alcohol' in the name, it is a fatty alcohol and is emollient/moisturizing, not drying
The main adverse effect is allergic contact dermatitis - relevant in patients with leg ulcers/stasis dermatitis
Used as an emulsifier, emulsion stabilizer, and stiffening agent in creams, ointments, and some tablets
Not an FDA-approved active drug; recognized as a pharmaceutical excipient (USP-NF) - guidance based on pharmacopeial/excipient sources
missed: Not applicable - cetyl alcohol has no therapeutic dosing schedule. For the finished emollient product, simply resume use as directed when needed.
overdose: Overdose is not a clinically relevant concept for topical cetyl alcohol. Accidental ingestion of large amounts may cause mild gastrointestinal upset; manage with supportive care.
